cards.prompt: A review sorter only saw **"cold"** in unhappy reviews, so it calls **"Lovely cold drinks"** unhappy. Best fix?

options.text: Add happy reviews that use "cold" in a nice way
Add more unhappy reviews that use "cold" too
Delete every training review with "cold" in it
Add 100 copies of one unhappy "cold" review

cards.explanation: It never saw "cold" used happily, so **add examples where it is**. More unhappy ones make it surer, and deleting them stops it spotting real cold-food complaints.

cards.prompt: A team rushes its labelling, and **1 in 10 dogs** is labelled "cat". What will this do to the model?

options.text: It learns some wrong lessons, so it mixes up more dogs
Nothing much: 9 in 10 labels are right, so it evens out
It notices the wrong labels by itself and skips them
It takes longer to train, then ends up just as good

cards.explanation: A model can't tell a wrong label from a right one, so each mislabelled dog teaches a **wrong lesson**. That's why labels should be **checked**, not rushed.

cards.prompt: A plant model is tested on **10** new photos. It gets **4 wrong**. What is its accuracy?
cards.explanation: It got 6 of the 10 right, and each photo is worth 10%: **60%**. Accuracy counts the ones it got **right**.

cards.prompt: A bird app scored **100%**, tested on the same photos it trained on. Is that a good test?

options.text: No: it may just have remembered those photos
Yes: 100% means it will never get a bird wrong
Yes, if the photos showed lots of different birds
No: a good test uses only the hardest bird photos

cards.explanation: Training photos only test **memory**: it may have **memorised them instead of learning**. A fair test uses photos it has **never seen**, easy and hard.

cards.prompt: Is each one a **fair** test of a model, or an **unfair** one?

items.label: Photos it never saw while training
Hard examples as well as easy ones
Photos in all kinds of light
Only the photos it already gets right

cards.explanation: Fair tests use **unseen**, **realistic** examples, easy and hard. Picking photos it gets right, or swapping photos until it scores 100%, flatters it.

cards.prompt: A face-matching app works well for adults but often fails on children. What is the **best** fix?

options.text: Add many photos of children, then test on children
Add many more photos of adults, then test again
Make the app accept every face much more easily
Report only its overall accuracy to users

cards.explanation: Children were missing from its training data, so it's **biased**: add them, then **test on children**. More adults, easier matching or one overall score don't fix that.

cards.prompt: A game's chat filter keeps blocking messages in one language that lots of players use.

steps.text: Those players get blocked even for normal messages. What should the game do?

choices.text: Ask those players to only write in English
choices.consequence: That blames the players. The problem is what the filter learned from.

choices.text: Train it on normal messages in that language, then test
choices.consequence: Right: fill the gap in the data, then check it really works for those players.

choices.text: Make the filter block fewer messages for everyone
choices.consequence: More mean messages get through, and it still doesn't understand that language.

cards.explanation: That language was missing from its training data. **Add the missing examples and test again**; never blame the people it gets wrong.

cards.prompt: Match each situation to the idea it shows.

pairs.left: Perfect on training, poor on new
Gets one accent right, not others

cards.explanation: **Test examples** are hidden while it learns, **accuracy** is the share right, perfect-then-poor means it **memorised**, and working worse for some people is **bias**.
